title: Alice & Bob Details QRMI and Slurm 26.11 Hierarchical Resource Integration for Cat-Qubit Systems at SC26 - Quantum Computing Report
gist: At SC26, Alice & Bob showed its cat-qubit processors plugging into NVIDIA's open-source Slurm 26.11 via the vendor-neutral QRMI interface, using Slurm's new native Hierarchical Resources (HRES) support instead of bespoke SPANK plugins. The work, from a year-long collaboration with STFC Hartree Centre plus IBM and Pasqal contributors, signals quantum-HPC integration consolidating on open, scheduler-agnostic standards.

insights.claim: Alice & Bob's cat-qubit quantum processors integrate with NVIDIA's open-source Slurm 26.11 workload manager through the vendor-neutral Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI), connecting its Felis cloud API directly to standard supercomputing schedulers without per-site custom software.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Lowers deployment friction for selling QPU access into HPC centers; watch for supercomputing-site adoption of cat-qubit systems.

insights.claim: Slurm 26.11 introduces native Hierarchical Resources (HRES) support with Lua plugin bindings that check availability, reserve access, configure compute nodes, and release resources at each stage of a hybrid quantum-classical job, replacing earlier bespoke SPANK plugins used to expose quantum hardware.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Native scheduler support turns quantum into a first-class HPC resource, shifting differentiation from integration plumbing to QPU performance.

insights.claim: Because Alice & Bob's cloud backend already implements the QRMI specification, its processors can move from SPANK-based Slurm clusters to the unified QRMI-HRES plugin without additional vendor-side integration work.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Early standard adopters get a free migration path, an advantage over QPU vendors still relying on custom per-site integrations.

insights.claim: Alice & Bob's QRMI implementation supports quantum workload scheduling across OpenPBS, IBM Spectrum LSF, Grid Engine, and Flux in addition to Slurm, plus an early-stage Kubernetes operator aimed at cloud-native clusters.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Broad scheduler coverage widens the addressable market from national HPC labs to enterprise and cloud-native environments.

insights.claim: A Kubernetes operator for QRMI is still early-stage, indicating quantum resource orchestration in cloud-native clusters lags maturity relative to traditional HPC schedulers.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Cloud-native quantum orchestration is an open gap; watch for maturation as a signal of enterprise-grade hybrid adoption.
insights.quote: an early-stage Kubernetes operator designed to extend quantum resource orchestration into cloud-native clusters

insights.claim: The QRMI-based architecture came out of a year-long collaboration between Alice & Bob and the UK's STFC Hartree Centre, with open-source contributors from IBM and Pasqal.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Competing QPU vendors co-developing shared middleware suggests the industry sees HPC integration as pre-competitive infrastructure.
insights.locator: Developed out of a year-long collaboration

insights.claim: At SC26, engineers from Alice & Bob, IBM, and Pasqal co-led a technical tutorial demonstrating workload-manager-agnostic QPU execution over QRMI, showing rival quantum hardware makers jointly promoting a vendor-neutral interface.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Standardization reduces lock-in for HPC buyers and could commoditize access layers, pushing competition toward qubit quality and scale.
insights.locator: At SC26, engineers from Alice & Bob
